baselineAnswer.text:
The encoder processes the images in order, taking one image at every timestep t; at t=5 the context vector is obtained through h_e^(t). [1]
The model's first component is an LSTM that summarizes the sequence of images; at t=5 it has encoded the 5 images and provides the sequence's context via its last hidden state h_e^(t). [2][3]
The model contains five independent decoders, one for each image in the sequence, and each decoder generates a sequence of words for its image; the final story is the concatenation of the five decoders' outputs. [4][5]
The first decoder generates words for the first image, the second decoder for the second image, and so on, allowing each decoder to learn a specific language model for each position of the sequence. [6][7]
All five decoders use the encoder's last hidden state as their first hidden state and take the corresponding image embedding as their first input. [8]

currentAnswer.text:
The encoder captures the sequence by taking the images in order, one at every timestep t; at time t=5 it obtains the context vector through h_e^(t) (represented by Z). [1][2]
The first component is an LSTM that summarizes the sequence of images: at every timestep t it takes as input an image I_i (i in {1,2,3,4,5}) from the sequence, and at t=5 it has encoded the 5 images and provides the sequence's context through its last hidden state h_e^(t). [3]
The model contains five independent decoders, one for each image in the sequence; all five use the encoder's last hidden state (the context) as their first hidden state and take the corresponding image embedding as their first input. [4][5]
The first decoder generates the words for the first image, the second decoder for the second image, and so on, so each decoder learns a specific language model for each position of the sequence. [4][6][7]
For example, the first decoder learns the opening sentences of the story while the last decoder learns the closing sentences. [4]
Each decoder generates a sequence of words for each image, and the final story is the concatenation of the output of the 5 decoders. [8][2]
The context vector initializes each decoder's hidden state, while each decoder's first input is its corresponding image embedding e(I_i). [9][2]
Having an independent decoder for each position of the image sequence allowed the visual storyteller to build more specific language models using the context vector as its first state and the image embedding as its first input. [10][11]

baselineAnswer.text:
The proposed BERT-based natural language generation model can be trained end-to-end without handcrafted features. [1]
The model uses a two-stage decoder process, in which each summary word is generated considering both sides' context information. [2]
During model training, the objective is the sum of the two processes, jointly trained using the "teacher-forcing" algorithm, feeding the ground-truth summary to each decoder and minimizing the objective. [3]
The model loss is defined as the sum of the decoder loss and the refine loss (L_model = L_dec + L_refine). [4]
Training uses an Adam optimizer with learning rate 3e-4, β1=0.9, β2=0.999, ε=1e-9, and a dynamic learning rate. [5]
Due to GPU memory limits, gradient accumulation is used with an accumulate step of 12 and 3 samples fed at each step. [6]
Training uses batch size 36 for 4 epochs (8 epochs for NYT50), with the best model selected from the last 10 models based on development set performance. [7]

The paper reviews the state of the art on conversational systems from three perspectives: types of interactions, types of architecture, and types of context reasoning, and consolidates them in a comparison table. [1]
For context reasoning, most proposed approaches in the state of the art rely on rules using logics and knowledge bases (the rule-oriented architecture). [2]
Three main types of architectures are identified for building conversational systems: totally rule-oriented, totally data-oriented, and a mix of rules and data-oriented. [3]
Most existing chatbots, from ELIZA to modern state-of-the-art ones, fall into the dyadic category. [4]
A dyadic chatbot does not know how to coordinate with many members in a chat group and lacks the social ability to know when it is more suitable to answer or not. [5]
The paper states there is a lack of methods and tools to design and engineer coordination and mediation among chatbots and humans. [6]
With regard to chatbot engines, there is a lack of research directed to building coordination laws integrated with natural language. [7]
The paper states its proposed architecture is, to the best of the authors' knowledge, the first in the state of the art designed to support coordinated aware chatbots in a multiparty conversation. [8]
The paper states it is not meant to advance the state of the art on the norms for MPCS. [9]

ELIZA 是早期理解自然语言处理的软件之一，由 Joseph Weizenbaum 于 1966 年在 MIT 创建，以扮演心理治疗师著称，只需反射病人的陈述。 [2]
ELIZA 旨在解决五个“基本技术问题”：识别关键词、发现最小上下文、选择适当变换、生成适当回应（有或无关键词时），以及为 ELIZA 脚本提供结束能力。 [3]
PARRY 紧随 ELIZA 之后，由斯坦福大学的精神病学家 Kenneth Colby 在 1970 年代初开发。 [4]
该程序用 MLISP 语言在 DEC PDP-10 的 WAITS 操作系统上编写，代码不可移植，部分用 PDP-10 汇编代码、部分用 MLISP 编写。 [5]
A.L.I.C.E. 于 1995 年出现，当前版本使用 AIML——一种为创建刺激-反应聊天机器人而设计的 XML 语言。 [6]
该程序无法通过图灵测试，因为即使是普通用户也常能在简短对话中暴露其机械性。 [7]
Cleverbot（1997-2014）是由英国 AI 科学家 Rollo Carpenter 开发的聊天机器人。 [8]
它通过了 2011 年图灵测试，该测试在印度理工学院古瓦哈提分校举办的 Technique Techno-Management Festival 上举行。 [9]
在最新技术中，大多数上下文推理方法依赖使用逻辑和知识库的规则，如规则导向架构小节所述。 [10]
构建对话系统主要有三类架构：完全规则导向、完全数据导向，以及规则与数据导向的混合。 [11]
大多数现有聊天机器人，从最早的 ELIZA 到现代最先进的系统，都属于这一类。 [12]
